lesson.title: @property: Attribute Syntax With Method Power
lesson.summary: The @property decorator lets a method be accessed with plain attribute syntax, obj.value instead of obj.value(), so a class can validate, compute, or protect a value while callers keep writing simple, uncluttered code.
lesson.body:
You already know how to write getter and setter methods by hand, functions like get_celsius() and set_celsius(value) that read and write an attribute while adding some logic around it, and you already understand decorators generally, functions that wrap another function to add behavior without rewriting its body, using the @ syntax placed just above a function definition. @property combines both ideas: it is a decorator, built into Python itself, whose job is to turn an ordinary method into something that callers access using plain attribute syntax, no parentheses, even though a method is genuinely running behind the scenes every time.

Why bother? Because Python culture favors direct attribute access, writing temp.celsius rather than temp.get_celsius(), for anything that conceptually is just a value on an object. But sometimes a value needs a rule attached to it. Maybe it needs validation, rejecting a temperature below absolute zero, for instance, or maybe it is not stored at all but computed on demand from other attributes, like a fahrenheit reading computed fresh from the stored celsius value every time it is asked for. @property lets you attach that logic to a method while still letting every caller use the clean attribute syntax they would use for a plain, unguarded attribute, and it means you can start with a plain attribute and add validation later without breaking any code that already uses obj.value.

```python
class Temperature:
    def __init__(self, celsius):
        self._celsius = celsius

    @property
    def celsius(self):
        return self._celsius

    @celsius.setter
    def celsius(self, value):
        if value < -273.15:
            raise ValueError("Temperature below absolute zero is impossible")
        self._celsius = value

    @property
    def fahrenheit(self):
        return self._celsius * 9 / 5 + 32

t = Temperature(25)
print(t.celsius)
print(t.fahrenheit)

t.celsius = 100
print(t.fahrenheit)

t.celsius = -300
```

The actual data lives in self._celsius, a plain attribute by convention treated as internal. The celsius property is the public getter: t.celsius silently calls that method and returns 25. fahrenheit is a read-only property, computed fresh every time from _celsius rather than stored separately, so it can never drift out of sync. The @celsius.setter decorated method fires whenever code writes t.celsius = something, letting the class validate the new value before accepting it. Running the first four statements prints:

```
25
77.0
212.0
```

25 degrees Celsius is 77.0 Fahrenheit, and after t.celsius = 100 updates the stored value, fahrenheit recomputes to 212.0, the boiling point. The final line, t.celsius = -300, runs the setter's validation check, negative 300 is below absolute zero, so the setter raises a ValueError with the message "Temperature below absolute zero is impossible" instead of silently accepting a physically impossible value, and the program stops with an unhandled exception. Every caller of this class still writes ordinary-looking attribute assignments and reads, t.celsius, not t.set_celsius(100), while the class quietly enforces its own rules behind that familiar syntax.
